ATTENTION IS ALL YOU NEED

A Foray Into Transformers

Marco R. Steenbergen
steenbergen@ipz.uzh.ch

University of Zurich

August 7, 2025

Motivation

Rich Embeddings

  • We have seen how Word2Vec and other methods generate embeddings by considering the context of a target word.

  • But that context is still limited to a few surrounding words.

  • What if we could take in a lot more context, e.g., all of a speech, law, or novel?

A Long Journey with a Happy End

  • It turns out that bringing in context is not easy, especially not when we try to use distal tokens to predict what is now.

  • Early efforts included

    • Recurrent neural networks.

    • Long short term memory.

  • Neither performed very well.

  • Finally, Vaswani et al. (2017) developed an elegant solution that has become the backbone of modern-day transformers such as BERT.

Recurrent Neural Networks

Mimicking Autoregressive Time Series

  • Consider the following sentence:

    The shrewd politician struck a major deal with her opponents.

  • We want to take into account how the first word continues to affect the last one.

  • We could mimic an AR(1) process:

    • “The” \(\rightarrow\) “shrewd” \(\rightarrow\) “politician” \(\rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow\) “her” \(\rightarrow\) “opponents”

  • OK, but we want to build this into a neural network to get embeddings.

We Have a Tool

  • Might this not be an excellent candidate for a recurrent neural network or RNN (Elman 1990)?
  • RNNs contain feedback loops have memory on the hidden states, which is exactly what we need.
  • They were developed for sequential data such as text or audio.

What Does RNN Look Like?

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville (2016), 373.

How Does That Help with Text?

t Word Input Hidden State
1 The \(x_1 = \text{Embed}(The)\) \(h_1 = f(x_1, h_0)\)
2 shrewd \(x_2 = \text{Embed}(shrewd)\) \(h_2 = f(x_2, h_1)\)
3 politician \(x_3 = \text{Embed}(politician)\) \(h_3 = f(x_3,h_2)\)
\(\cdots\) \(\cdots\) \(\cdots\) \(\cdots\)
11 opponents \(x_{11} = \text{Embed}(opponents)\) \(h_{11} = f(x_{11}, h_{10})\)

In theory, the word “The” is carried forward because it flows into \(h_1\), which flows into \(h_2\), etc. The same holds true for later words and their subsequent effects.

Numeric Example

  • Setup
  • Setup Cont’d
  • Step 1
  • Step 2
  • Interpretation

Imagine a tiny RNN with

  • 2D word embeddings

  • 2D hidden states

  • No bias

  • A \(\tanh\) activation

  • Let \(x_1^\top = [1,0]\) and \(x_2^\top = [0,1]\) for illustrating the first two words.

  • Assume \(h_0^\top = [0,0]\).

  • Let

    \[ W_x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \ \text{and} \ W_h = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • We update using \(h_t = \tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1})\).

\[ h_1 = \tanh \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \right) \approx \begin{bmatrix} 0.76 \\ 0.76 \end{bmatrix} \]

\[ h_2 = \tanh \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.76 \\ 0.76 \end{bmatrix} \right) \approx \begin{bmatrix} 0.88 \\ -0.55 \end{bmatrix} \]

Step Word Hidden State Meaning
0 START \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \] No context yet.
1 “The” \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0.76 \\ 0.76 \end{bmatrix} \] Encodes info about “The.”
2 “shrewd” \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0.88 \\ -0.55 \end{bmatrix} \] Reflects both “The” and “shrewd” in compressed form.

Trouble in Paradise

  • Hochreiter (1991) documented the problem of vanishing gradients in RNNs.
  • That is, the gradients become vanishingly smallas we engage in backpropagation through time.
  • This has two downsides:
    1. Backpropagation frequently fails.
    2. Even if it succeeds, it is not clear how much the distal past still matters for the current word (memory loss).

Why Vanishing Gradients Happen

  • For simplicity, let \(h_t = W_h h_{t-1}\).

  • We define a loss function \(L = \ell(h_T)\).

  • We seek to update the weights and for that we need

    \[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_h} = \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_t} \cdot \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial W_h} \]

  • However \(\partial h_t/\partial W_h = h_{t-1}^\top \otimes I\).

  • Consequently, \(\partial L/\partial W_h = \sum_{t=1}^T \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_T} \cdot W_h^{T-t} \right) h_{t-1}^\top\).

  • If \(||W_h|| < 1\) then \(\lim_{T-t \rightarrow \infty} W_h^{T-t} = 0\).

  • The model cannot learn from earlier inputs.

LSTM to the Rescue

  • Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) built an algorithm that seeks to bypass these problems: long short term memory.

  • This remembers information over long time spans.

  • It avoids vanishing gradients through several mechanisms:

    • Cell states act like memory conveyor belts—information can flow through many time steps with minimal modification.

    • Gates (input, forget, output) control what information is added, keptm or removed from the memory.

    • The update mechanism is additive rather than multiplicative.

But It Is Not Enough

  • Works well for moderate-length sequences (50-100 tokens).

  • Long documents (500+ tokens) still yield problems because memory cells still get overwritten.

  • Perhaps following a sequential logic is not good enough.

Attention Is All You Need

Vaswani et al.’s Breakthrough

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) tell us to forget about sequence.

  • Let each token attend to any other token regardless of position.

  • Use this attention to update a set of embeddings.

  • One can even run many of these attention mechanisms in parallel \(\rightarrow\) multi-head attention.

The Intuition

  • Every token starts with an initial embedding.

    • E.g., “house” will be represented in the embedding space near “villa,” “home,” etc.

  • We update that embedding based on the context of the word.

    • E.g., “little house” might change the embedding of “house,” moving it perhaps away from “villa.”

    • E.g., “little house on the prairie” will change the embedding even more because “house” now is part of the title of a 1970s American TV series.

The Initial Embedding Space

We start with a high-dimensional vector containing the embeddings of each token. For instance,

\[ \begin{array}{ccccc} \text{The} & \text{shrewd} & \text{politician} & \cdots & \text{opponents} \\ \downarrow & \downarrow & \downarrow & & \downarrow \\ E_1 & E_2 & E_3 & \cdots & E_{10} \end{array} \]

Here, \(E\) may have 1024 elements, as in BERT large.

The Key Formula

Vaswani et al. (2017) proposed that the updates to the embeddings are given by

\[ \text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax} \left( \frac{K^\top Q}{\sqrt{d}} \right) V \]

Example of Attention

  • Imagine we are interested in the way in which adjectives alter the meaning of words.

  • In the sentence, “The shrewd politician struck a major deal with her opponents,” this amounts to asking

    • How does “shrewd” affect the meaning of “politician.”

    • How does “major” affect the meaning of “deal.”

  • Important: In reality we do not have that much control over what attention heads do; it is just to show the logic.

The Query

  • Imagine the noun “politician” asking whether any adjectives are placed in front of it.

  • We would expect “shrewd” to answer “yes.”

  • The question is encoded as the query.

    • This is another vector but its dimensionality is less than that of the original embeddings!

  • We compute the query as a matrix-vector product. For “politician,” which is in position 3, this becomes \(W_Q E_3 = Q_3\).

    • Here \(W_Q\) is a matrix of trainable weights

  • We do this for all tokens simultaneously. For the \(i\)th token,

    \[ Q_i = W_Q E_i \]

The Keys

  • We also encode the answers to the queries; they become the keys.

  • So for instance, “shrewd” also is transformed using \(W_K E_2 = K_2\).

    • Here \(W_K\) is another trainable weight matrix.

  • As before, the process occurs simultaneously for all embeddings. Hence,

    \[ K_j = W_K E_j \]

Bringing Keys and Queries Together

  • So how well does each key speak to a query?

  • The mathematical vehicle for answering that question is the dot product

    \[ K_j Q_i \]

  • Its value indicates how relevant the key is to the query.

  • For instance, if “politician” asked which adjective comes before me, then we would expect \(K_2 Q_3\) to be particularly large.

  • We say: the embedding of “shrewd” attends to the embedding of “politician.”

Bring Keys and Queries Together Cont’d

\[ \begin{bmatrix} & \text{The} & \text{shrew} & \text{politician} & \cdots & \text{opposition} \\ \text{The} & K_1 Q_1 & K_1Q_2 & K_1Q_3 & \cdots & K_1Q_{10} \\ \text{shrewd} & K_2 Q1 & K_2 Q_2 & K_2 Q_3 & \cdots & K_2 Q_{10} \\ \text{politician} & K_3 Q_1 & K_3 Q_2 & K_3 Q_3 & \cdots & K_3 Q_{10} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \text{opposition} & K_{10} Q_1 & K_{10} Q_2 & K_{10} Q_3 & \cdots & K_{10} Q_{10} \end{bmatrix} \]

Vaswani et al. (2017) write \(K^\top Q\) for this key-query matrix.

The Softmax Function

  • In each column, we have a series of values that show the relevance of each key for the token in the column

  • At the moment these are real numbers that Vaswani et al. (2017) divide by the square root of the dimensionality (number of rows), \(d\), of the key-query space.

  • But would not it be nice to render these numbers as probabilities that add to 1 in each column?

  • This is done through the softmax function, which is applied for each column.

  • The resulting space is called the attention pattern.

    • Tells us with context words contribute to the representation of the target word.

Almost There

  • With \(N\) tokens, the attention pattern is a \(N \times N\) matrix, at least if we allow each word to speak to each other word.

  • The original embedding space, had a different dimensionality, e.g., \(1024 \times N\).

  • To update the embeddings we need to transform the attention pattern to be conformable with the attention space.

  • This is where \(V\) (values) come into the picture

    • Also trained.

    • Multiplied by the weights and summed.

    • Give the adjustments to the embeddings.

  • The final embedding is the original embedding plus the adjustment.

  • We have transformed the embedding \(\rightarrow\) a transformer was born.

Attention Is Not All You Need After All

Almost There and Yet So Far Away

  • We got rid off sequence, but does it not still matter? Do not words come in a particular order?

  • Transformers process tokens in parallel.

  • This is faster, but we lose positional information that is highly relevant.

  • We need to add positional encoding to make this work.

The Problem

  • You might think positional encoding is as simple as assigning integers such as 0 for “The”, 1 for “shrewd,” etc.

  • But neural networks do not know what to do with this:

    • No generalization across different sequence lengths.

    • No sense of ordinality.

    • Relatedly, the integers do not preserve relative or global structure because they may undergo linear transformations.

  • Moreover, we may want positional encodings to be sensitive to different rythms:

    • Slow—capturing coarse distances such as beginning versus end.

    • Fast—capturing fine distances such as token versus token.

Positional Encoding Done Right

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) proposed

    \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \text{PE}_{\text{pos},2i} &=& \sin \left( \frac{\text{pos}}{10000^{\frac{2i}{d_m}}} \right) \\ \text{PE}_{\text{pos},2i + 1} &=& \cos \left( \frac{\text{pos}}{10000^{\frac{2i}{d_m}}} \right) \end{array} \]

  • We settle on a number of positional encodings, \(d_m\), where \(m\) is the model.

  • We take positional information (integers) \(\text{pos}\).

  • \(i\) is a frequency index.

  • If the dimension is even, then the sine-formula is used; otherwise the cosine-formula.

Illustration

  • The word “politician” occurs in \(\text{pos} = 3\).

  • Imagine, \(d_m = 6\); we opt for two positional encodings.

  • Then \(i = 0, 1, 2\) because each \(i\) produces 2 dimensions, even and odd.

  • So \(i = 0\) produces

    \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \sin \left( \frac{3}{10000^{\frac{0}{6}}} \right) &=& \sin(3) \\ \cos \left( \frac{3}{10000^{\frac{0}{6}}} \right) &=& \cos(3) \end{array} \]

Determinism versus Learning

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) opted for fixed positional encodings.

  • Later algorithms like BERT have turned this into a training problem \(\rightarrow\) typically better performance.

Encoders and Decoders

The Full Architecture

Source: Vaswani et al. (2017), 3. The encoder is shown on the left; the decoder on the right. The latter was used for a translation task.

Encoder-Decoder Logic

  • Encoders make sense of text \(\rightarrow\) embeddings and positional encodings:

    • The encoder turns an input sequence of tokens (e.g., a sentence) into a sequence of contextualized vectors—one per token—that carry rich semantic and positional information.

  • Decoders use this information to answer specific questions like:

    • Who was Julius Caesar?

    • How do I translate “I hate spinach” into French?

    • What is the derivative of \(\ln(x^2)\)?

    • What is the Python code for a CNN?

Multi-Head Attention

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) employed multi-head attention:

    • Instead of generating one attention pattern, we generate many.

  • Multi-head attention allows the model to learn diverse relationships in parallel, just like CNNs use multiple filters to detect features.

  • This is a standard feature of transformers.

What Is Going on in the Encoder?

  1. Input embeddings (a.k.a. static embeddings) are fed from an embedding table.
  2. Positional encodings are generated.
  3. The encoder block processes the input embeddings and positional encodings and is repeated \(N\) times.
  4. Output embeddings are generated.

The Encoder Block

  1. Multi-head attention mechanisms run in parallel and allow for specialization.
  2. We add the input vector to the attention output (residual connection) to obtain updated embeddings and then norm for stabilization.
  3. A small multi-layer perceptron is applied independently to each token’s vector, allowing the model to mix and transform the features learned from attention.
  4. A residual connection and normalization are once more applied.
